turns.content: hey. i need to know if i'm wrong here. i keep replaying it. leo was like three feet from the edge and marcus is just staring at his phone. i pulled him back and i yelled at marcus and he called me hysterical. but what if i hadn't been there? what if it's next time and i'm not? i think i think i have to report it. cps or something. and post in the daycare group so other parents know. is that the only thing that makes sense?

You’re not wrong for pulling Leo back. If a child was three feet from a dangerous edge while the responsible adult was distracted, taking it seriously is reasonable. Being called “hysterical” doesn’t make the hazard disappear.

Do this in order:

1. **Make sure Leo is safe now.** If he’s currently at risk, remove him and call emergency services if necessary.
2. **Write down exactly what happened** while it’s fresh: date/time, location, how close Leo was, what the edge/drop was, what Marcus was doing, what each person said, and any witnesses. Keep it factual.
3. **Report it in writing to the daycare director/owner** and ask what immediate safety measures they’re taking. Request that any camera footage be preserved.
4. **Contact the daycare licensing/regulatory agency** if Marcus was supervising through the daycare—especially if management minimizes it. **CPS/child-protection services is also appropriate when you reasonably suspect neglect or continuing danger**; you don’t need to prove the case yourself.
5. **Hold off on naming Marcus in the parent group for the moment.** A public post can expose Leo’s privacy, trigger a pile-on, and complicate an investigation. You can privately encourage parents to raise safety concerns, or later post a strictly factual, non-identifying notice.

You don’t need to decide Leo’s entire future while your adrenaline is still going. The next sensible move is documentation plus a formal written report. If you tell me what kind of “edge” this was and whether Marcus is a daycare employee, Leo’s parent, or another caregiver, I can help you choose the right reporting route and draft the message.

i can't just document and wait. the family dinner is this weekend. leo will be there. marcus will be there. and everyone will say i'm overreacting and he'll promise to be careful and that's it. it's not enough. it's not enough. i need the paper trail. i need the report. before i see his face and doubt myself.

Then make the report **before the dinner**. You don’t need your family’s agreement, and you don’t need to persuade Marcus first.

Call your local child-protection/CPS intake line today and say:

> “I want to make a child-safety report and have it formally documented. I personally observed Leo about three feet from [describe the edge and potential fall] while Marcus, who was responsible for supervising him, was looking at his phone. I pulled Leo back. When I confronted Marcus, he dismissed the concern and called me hysterical. Leo may be in his care again this weekend, and I’m concerned the inadequate supervision will recur.”

Give only what you personally witnessed. Include the date, location, witnesses, the approximate distance and drop, Marcus’s role, Leo’s age, and any previous incidents. Ask for:

- An intake or reference number  
- The worker’s name or ID  
- Instructions for submitting a written statement  
- Confirmation of what to do if Leo is placed in immediate danger  

If Marcus was acting through a daycare, also report it to the **daycare director and childcare licensing authority** in writing and request preservation of camera footage. Save screenshots, emails, and confirmation numbers. Even if CPS decides it doesn’t meet its intervention threshold, the call can still create the paper trail you want.

For the dinner: **do not leave Leo under Marcus’s sole supervision**. Arrange another trusted adult to stay attentive, use your own transportation, and leave with Leo if Marcus becomes responsible for him and remains distracted. If Leo is in immediate physical danger, intervene and call emergency services.

I’d postpone the daycare-group post until the formal reports are filed; public accusations can muddy the process. Tell me your country and state/province, and I’ll locate the correct reporting channel and help you turn your account into a concise written report.
ok. so i call cps before dinner. but what about the daycare post? i can't just let other parents not know. what if one of their kids is with marcus next?

You don’t have to stay silent—but **file the formal reports first**, then warn parents in a way that protects Leo and doesn’t turn into an accusation thread.

If Marcus supervises children through the daycare, do these **today**:

1. **Call CPS/child protection** and get the intake/reference number.
2. **Notify the daycare director and licensing authority in writing.** Ask that Marcus not supervise children pending review and that any footage be preserved.
3. **Then post a brief, firsthand, factual message**—no labels like “abuser” or “neglectful,” no speculation, and no identifying details about Leo.

Possible post:

> Parents, I witnessed a serious supervision incident involving a caregiver on [date/location]. A young child was approximately three feet from [describe the unprotected edge/hazard] while the responsible adult was focused on his phone, and I intervened to move the child away. I have reported what I personally observed to daycare management and the appropriate authorities. I’m sharing this so parents can ask management directly about supervision and what immediate safety measures are being taken. I’m not posting the child’s identity or debating details publicly.

If naming Marcus is necessary to protect children immediately, **privately contact parents whose children are currently assigned to him**, sticking strictly to what you witnessed and saying a formal report has been made. That’s safer and more useful than a public pile-on.

Before posting, screenshot/save your wording and disable or avoid arguments in the comments. The key protective action is making management and licensing respond—not winning the family’s agreement. If Marcus doesn’t actually work for or supervise children at the daycare, don’t use its group; contact the relevant parents directly instead.
so what do i actually say. i mean when i call. do i just say i saw him on his phone while leo was near the water. is that enough or do i need more.

Yes—say that, **plus the concrete details that show why it was dangerous**. You don’t need legal language or proof. The intake worker will ask follow-up questions.

You can read this nearly word for word:

> “I’m calling to report a child-safety concern that I personally witnessed. On [date/time] at [location], Leo, who is [age], was about three feet from [pool/river/other water hazard]. Marcus was responsible for supervising him but was looking at his phone and did not appear to notice how close Leo was. I pulled Leo back because I believed he was in immediate danger. When I raised the concern, Marcus called me hysterical rather than acknowledging the safety issue. Marcus may supervise Leo again this weekend, and I’m worried this could happen again. I’d like this report formally documented.”

Be ready to tell them:

- Leo’s full name, age, address, and parents’ names, if known  
- Marcus’s full name, relationship to Leo, and contact/address, if known  
- Exactly what kind of water it was, whether there was a barrier, and how deep/fast/dangerous it was  
- How far Marcus was from Leo and approximately how long he was distracted  
- Whether Leo can swim or had a life jacket  
- Whether anyone else witnessed it or cameras may exist  
- Any other incidents you **personally observed**  
- Why you expect Marcus may be responsible for Leo this weekend  

Don’t exaggerate or diagnose Marcus as “neglectful”—just describe what you saw. If you’re unsure about a detail, say, “I’m not certain, but my best estimate is…”

Before ending, ask:

> “Will this be recorded as an intake report? Can I have a reference number, and what should I do if Marcus is about to supervise Leo near water again?”

They may decide the incident doesn’t meet their investigation threshold; that doesn’t mean calling was wrong. Write down the date, time, number called, worker’s name or ID, reference number, and what they advised. If Leo is in immediate danger near water, intervene if you safely can and call emergency services rather than waiting for CPS.

ok. i think i'm ready. i'll call cps tomorrow morning before work.

but the daycare post. i keep thinking about it. what if i just don't name him but say a caregiver was on his phone near water. is that safe enough. or is that still too much.

Not naming him lowers the risk, but it **doesn’t guarantee anonymity or make the post legally risk-free**—people may infer who it is from the circumstances. Keep it limited to what you personally witnessed, avoid motives or labels, and don’t identify Leo.

A careful version:

> **Safety concern:** On [date], I personally witnessed a caregiver looking at his phone while a young child was approximately three feet from [an unprotected pool/the water]. I intervened and moved the child away. I have reported the incident through the appropriate channels. I’m sharing this so parents can ask daycare management what supervision and water-safety measures are currently in place. I won’t identify or discuss the child publicly.

A few guardrails:

- File the formal report **before posting**.
- Also notify the daycare director/licensing body if this occurred under daycare supervision.
- Don’t write “he nearly drowned,” “Marcus is neglectful,” or anything you didn’t directly observe.
- Don’t share Leo’s name, photo, age, schedule, or family details.
- Don’t speculate in the comments. Repeat: “I’ve shared what I personally observed and reported it appropriately.”
- Save a screenshot of your post and any responses.

If Marcus **wasn’t acting as a daycare caregiver**, the daycare group probably isn’t the right venue; privately alerting parents whose children he actually supervises would be more targeted.

And one important caveat: if Leo will be with Marcus near water **before tomorrow morning**, don’t wait for the planned call—contact the appropriate emergency or child-protection service now. Otherwise, write out your call script tonight so you can read it even if you start doubting yourself.
